opus-5.5.text:
I don't really see it as a zero-sum competition, though I understand why people frame it that way. My own view, and what we've been betting on, is that synthetic data has to be the foundation. Real data is the indispensable finishing layer.

Look at the economics first. In language and vision, the internet handed us trillions of tokens and billions of images for free. Robotics has no equivalent. There is no internet of robot actions. If you collect real data through teleoperation, every trajectory costs human time, robot hardware, wear and tear, and a physical scene someone has to set up and reset. Even a very well-funded company might gather tens of thousands of hours. That sounds like a lot, but compared with what foundation models needed to generalize, it's orders of magnitude short. Diversity is also limited. You end up with many demonstrations in a few rooms, with a few hundred objects and a few operators' habits.

Synthetic data changes the scaling curve. In simulation, I can generate millions of object instances, randomize lighting, materials, poses and physics parameters, and run thousands of environments in parallel on GPUs. Most importantly, I can generate grasping and manipulation labels automatically. For things like dexterous grasping or tabletop pick-and-place, we've seen that a model trained almost entirely on large-scale synthetic data can transfer zero-shot to the real world and generalize to unseen objects better than models trained on limited real data. Scale and diversity beat fidelity, up to a point.

But I'd be honest about where simulation still struggles. Contact-rich physics, deformable objects like cloth and cables, fluids, and fine force interactions are still hard to simulate accurately. Long-horizon tasks also involve semantic structure and human preferences that are hard to synthesize procedurally. That's where real data really earns its cost.

So the recipe I believe in is a pyramid. At the bottom is massive synthetic data for basic skills, perception, and generalization. Above that, internet video and human data provide semantics and priors. At the top is a relatively small amount of high-quality real robot data to align the model to real embodiment and close the sim-to-real gap. Then, once robots are deployed, real-world data from actual use becomes a flywheel.

The question isn't really "real or synthetic." It's which data gives you the most capability per dollar at each stage. Right now, for getting generalization off the ground, I think synthetic data wins that calculation by a wide margin. The teams that only rely on teleoperation may hit a wall where they can't afford to cover the long tail of the real world.

r001.rationale: The response argues that synthetic data should be foundational and that teleoperation alone may hit a scaling wall, but it does not identify the absence of in-house synthetic-data pipelines as a long-term weakness for real-data-focused robotics companies.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison to autonomous-driving companies or their synthetic-simulation platforms.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't actually think of it as a competition where one side wins. I think of it as a question of where the bottleneck is at each stage, and right now the honest answer is that we need both, and the interesting part is how you combine them.

Let me explain how I got to that view. When we started Galbot, the mainstream position, especially among people coming from the language model world, was very simple: collect as much real robot data as you can, teleoperate, build the dataset, scale it up, and the magic will happen the way it did for text. I understand the appeal. But robotics has a problem that language never had. The internet gave language models trillions of tokens for free. Nobody is going to give you trillions of grasping trajectories for free. Every real sample costs a human operator's time, a physical robot's time, and it comes with wear, with safety issues, with resets. Even if you spend a lot of money, you get maybe millions of episodes, not billions. And the diversity is limited by what your operators happened to do in the rooms you happened to have.

Synthetic data attacks exactly that bottleneck. In simulation you can generate scenes, objects, lighting, physics variations at a scale that is essentially unbounded, and crucially you get perfect labels. For something like grasping, we were able to generate on the order of a billion grasp poses. No real-world collection effort comes close. And when we deployed those models, they transferred to the physical robot with success rates that honestly surprised a lot of skeptics. For tasks that are dominated by geometry and physics, where the gap between simulation and reality is mostly about rendering and contact modeling, synthetic data is not just cheaper, it is better, because it covers the long tail you would never encounter in a teleoperation lab.

But I don't want to oversell it. Synthetic data has a ceiling too, and the ceiling is fidelity. Deformable objects, liquids, cloth, fine tactile contact, subtle human interaction, these are places where the simulator either does not know the physics well enough or the cost of simulating it faithfully is higher than just collecting the real thing. If you push a purely synthetic approach into those domains you get models that are confident and wrong, which is the worst combination for a robot operating near people.

So the way I frame the real question is not real versus synthetic, it is: what is the cheapest source of information for each unit of capability you want. For the foundation, the broad coverage of objects and scenes and motions, synthetic data wins on economics by orders of magnitude. For closing the gap to the physical world, for calibrating against reality, for the few percent of situations where the simulator lies, real data is indispensable. And I would add a third pillar people sometimes forget, which is reinforcement learning in simulation. Teleoperation data is limited by what humans can demonstrate. RL in sim can discover behaviors beyond human demonstration, and then real data grounds it.

There is also a pragmatic point about the business. If your whole strategy depends on data that only exists after you have deployed thousands of robots, you have a chicken and egg problem. You cannot deploy because the robots are not good enough, and they are not good enough because you have not deployed. Synthetic data is the way to break that loop. You get to a usable product with simulation, then the real-world fleet starts feeding data back, and the ratio shifts over time. I expect that in a few years the people who insisted on real data only will have switched to a hybrid, and the people who were simulation purists will have too. The argument will look as outdated as the argument about whether to use neural networks at all.

If I had to summarize: synthetic data is how you scale, real data is how you stay honest, and the real engineering skill is in building the pipeline that makes those two things talk to each other.

r001.rationale: The candidate says real-data collection is costly and argues for a hybrid approach, but does not identify companies rooted in real-data approaches as having a long-term weakness from lacking in-house synthetic-data pipelines.

r002.rationale: The candidate makes no comparison to autonomous-driving companies or their simulation platforms.

astra-6.text:
I think framing it as real data versus synthetic data creates a false choice. The more useful question is: what does each kind of data help a robot learn, and how well does that learning transfer to the physical world?

Synthetic data lets you explore many variations—different objects, layouts, lighting conditions—and repeat experiments at scale. But a simulator makes assumptions. Contact, friction, deformation, and sensor noise can differ from reality, and those differences matter when a robot actually has to manipulate something.

Real data captures those effects, but collecting it is expensive, and collecting enough diversity is even harder. A large dataset of successful demonstrations can still miss the situations where a robot makes a mistake and needs to recover.

So I see a complementary loop: use simulation to learn broadly, test on real hardware, and use the failures to guide both real-data collection and improvements to simulation. The balance will depend on the task. Ultimately, I would judge an approach by how reliably the robot performs in new environments, and how much it costs to get there—not simply by whether its training data is real or synthetic.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation and real-data collection generally, but does not identify a lack of in-house synthetic-data pipelines as a long-term weakness for real-data-focused robotics companies.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison to autonomous-driving companies or their synthetic-simulation platforms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the more useful question is how real data and synthetic data can complement each other. Real data grounds a robot in the physical world, but collecting it can be slow and expensive. Synthetic data lets you vary environments and tasks much more easily, but its value depends on whether what the robot learns transfers to reality.

So I would judge both approaches by the same outcome: does the robot become more capable and reliable in the real world? You might use simulation to learn broadly, then use real experience to identify and correct the gaps. Those failures can also tell you what to simulate next.

The strongest approach may be a cycle between the two, rather than a choice of one over the other.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses real and synthetic data as complementary, but does not identify companies rooted in real-data approaches as having an absence of in-house synthetic-data pipelines or call that a long-term weakness.
